You’re absolutely right—desert wind can be a real challenge for field audio, especially when you’re trying to capture clear observations on the fly. It’s great that Emily flagged the wind noise early; catching those issues in the notes will save you a lot of time later.

**Here are some practical tips for cleaning up your field audio:**

**1. Use a High-Pass Filter:**  
Most wind noise is low-frequency rumble. Applying a high-pass filter (start around 80–120 Hz) in software like Audacity, Adobe Audition, or even some free online tools can cut out a lot of the unwanted noise without affecting voices too much.

**2. Noise Reduction Tools:**  
Most audio editors have noise reduction features. You can sample a section of “just wind” and let the software subtract that pattern from the rest of the recording. Audacity’s “Noise Reduction” effect is a good starting point.

**3. Manual Editing:**  
If the wind is intermittent, you can manually lower the volume or mute those sections. Sometimes, splitting the audio into short clips and only keeping the cleanest bits is the most practical approach.

**4. Spectral Editing:**  
If you have access to advanced tools (like iZotope RX), spectral editing lets you visually isolate and remove wind bursts without harming the spoken parts.

**5. EQ Tweaks:**  
Boosting the midrange (where voices sit) and cutting the lows can help voices stand out over wind. Just be careful not to make the audio sound too thin.

**6. Future Field Tips:**  
- If you’re using handheld recorders, try foam windscreens or even DIY “dead cat” covers (furry windshields).
- Position the mic so it’s shielded by your body or a notebook.
- Record a few seconds of “ambient wind” at each site—this helps with noise profiling later.

**For your current files:**  
Start with a high-pass filter and noise reduction. If the wind is really bad, you might need to transcribe by ear and use the audio only for reference, but often you can salvage more than you expect.
